title: Supervisor Essentials for Water and Wastewater Operators
audience: Operators, lead operators and new supervisors across the US and Canada who are moving into or preparing for a supervisory role in water or wastewater work.
prerequisites: No technical prerequisite beyond basic arithmetic and a calculator. All scenarios, names, utilities and dollar figures are fictional. Certification, staffing and employment rules differ between states and provinces, so the course teaches general principles and tells you to check your state's or province's rules.
introduction: Build the habits of a good first-line supervisor: how the role differs from operating, what responsibility and accountability mean, how management styles and organisation charts shape the crew, and how to lead people through change and problems. Each module has worked examples, quick checks that name the mistakes behind wrong answers, and a short written case. The course gives general supervision principles, not any jurisdiction's rules, and safety content is recognition and purpose only; facility procedures govern.
delivery: Self-paced lessons, optional quick checks, a graded final exam and a non-credit certificate. Duration is being validated; no contact-hour award is made.

### Fictional scenario: Marisol's first month

Marisol Ortega has just been promoted to day-shift supervisor at the fictional Cedar Flats Water Authority. As an operator she spent 34 of her 40 paid hours on hands-on work. Her first-month time log shows 15 hands-on hours. A former crew mate, Rui, asks her to leave a late entry out of the log. A second operator, Dev, has been late three times and she never mentioned it when they were peers. Her manager has not yet told her what she may approve.

### Your decision

Decide how Marisol should use her time, what she says to Rui and Dev, and what she must clarify with her manager.
modules.assignment: Write a one-page plan for Marisol's second month. Calculate the share of her week that is hands-on now and the hours that moved away from hands-on work, name three supervising tasks that should fill them, write two or three sentences she could say to Rui, and list three questions for her manager about the limits of her authority. Do not state any hiring or firing power as given; say it varies.
rubric: Fills the freed hours with supervising tasks such as assigning, checking, coaching and recording, not more hands-on work.
Keeps the log accurate, applies the same standard to Rui and Dev, and stays respectful.
Asks about overtime, scheduling and discipline limits and notes that hiring and firing authority varies by employer.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Before: 34 / 40 = 85 percent hands-on. Now: 15 / 40 = 37.5 percent. Hours moved: 34 - 15 = 19. Accept any sensible supervising tasks. Look for a private, consistent response to Rui (the log must match events, same rule for everyone) and a documented conversation with Dev rather than a one-off favour or a public warning. modules.lesson: ### From doing the work to getting the work done Many supervisors in water and wastewater start as skilled operators. They read the gauges, adjust the feed, fix the fault and finish the log. Promotion rewards that skill, and then changes what the job asks for. A supervisor is responsible for the day-to-day performance of a small group, such as a shift or a crew. Success is measured by what the group gets done safely and correctly, not by how much one person does personally. That change is harder than it sounds. The new supervisor's instinct is to jump in and fix things, because fixing is what made them valuable. Every hour spent repairing a pump while the crew waits for direction is an hour the supervisor was not assigning work, checking quality or writing the record. The work moves from doing, to assigning, guiding, monitoring and documenting. ### What a supervisor is, and where the role sits In plain terms, a supervisor guides a group toward its goals and sees that each member is productive. The word has a dictionary meaning, which is a person who oversees the work of others, and a legal and employment meaning that is stricter. In many employment settings the legal test looks at real authority and independent judgement over other workers, not at the title on a business card. A person called "senior supervisor" who cannot assign work or recommend discipline may not be a supervisor in the legal sense, and a person with no such title who regularly directs a crew may be. Legal tests differ between jurisdictions and between laws, so check the rules that apply to your employer; a labour agreement may separately set out the duties and limits of the role. On an organisation chart the supervisor usually sits above the operators and below a manager. That middle position has two directions of accountability. Upward, the supervisor answers to the manager for results, records and safety on the shift. Downward, the supervisor answers to the crew for clear direction, fair treatment, training and the tools to do the work. A supervisor who only looks upward becomes a messenger; one who only looks downward becomes one of the crew again. ### What authority a supervisor usually has Authority varies by utility, so a new supervisor should ask for the limits in writing. Common patterns are listed here, and none of them is guaranteed. - Assigning daily tasks and adjusting the work schedule within policy and any labour agreement. - Directing how and when work is carried out, and stopping work that looks unsafe or improperly done. - Evaluating performance, giving feedback and recommending training. - Starting or recommending discipline, often with the manager or human resources taking the final step. - Hiring, firing, promotion and pay decisions, which vary widely. In many organisations the supervisor interviews or recommends and a manager decides. Typical limits sit above the role: proposing or setting rates, approving capital budgets, applying for permit changes and agreeing contracts usually belong to a manager, a general manager, a governing board or a council. The permit conditions themselves are changed only by the permitting authority. Knowing where your authority ends is part of the job. Acting beyond it creates problems for you and the utility, and refusing to use the authority you do have leaves the crew without direction. ### Former peers, fairness and consistency Yesterday's coworker is today's direct report. Some will be glad for you; some may have wanted the promotion. A few expect that old favours and shortcuts still apply. The most useful habit is consistency: hold every member of the crew to the same standards, apply the same rules about records, attendance and safe practice, and give the same kind of feedback whether the person is a close friend or a stranger. Favouritism, even when it feels like kindness, is quickly noticed and damages trust in the whole crew. Consistency does not mean coldness. You can stay friendly and still be clear that the role has changed. A good way to start is a short conversation with each person, one at a time, about what you will expect, what they can expect from you, and how you will handle problems. Do not apologise for the promotion and do not hand out special treatment to win people over. ### Supervisor, lead operator and manager compared These titles are used loosely, so compare duties, not names. - **Lead operator:** works hands-on and guides peers on technical tasks. The authority is often informal, and there may be no disciplinary power. - **Supervisor:** directs the daily work and records of a group, assigns work, evaluates performance and is usually involved in discipline. - **Manager:** plans, budgets and reports for a wider area, with authority over staffing plans and spending limits inside the policy the board or council sets. A lead operator is often the stepping stone: the role gives practice at guiding others while still doing technical work. A manager has a longer time horizon, thinking in months and budgets, where the supervisor thinks in shifts and weeks. ### Worked example: a week that changes shape Marisol Ortega is promoted to day-shift supervisor at the fictional Cedar Flats Water Authority. As an operator she spent 34 of her 40 paid hours on hands-on work: rounds, adjustments, minor repairs and sampling. After a month as supervisor, still paid for a 40-hour week, she records her hours. Hands-on work has dropped to 15 hours. The rest of the week is split between assigning and following up on work, coaching, meetings with the manager, scheduling and records. Step 1: share of the week hands-on before = 34 hours / 40 hours x 100 = 85 percent. Step 2: share hands-on now = 15 hours / 40 hours x 100 = 37.5 percent. Step 3: hours moved away from hands-on work = 34 - 15 = 19 hours per week. Those 19 hours did not disappear. They now go to the supervising tasks that no one else on the shift is doing. If Marisol keeps 85 percent hands-on after promotion, the crew has a very good operator and no supervisor, and the planning, coaching and records will not get done. In her second week an old crew mate asks her to leave a late entry out of the log because "we always did it this way." Marisol answers in private: the log has to match what happened, the same expectation applies to everyone including her, and she is happy to help him fix the reason the entry was late. She does not agree to a one-off exception, and, because Cedar Flats policy lets a supervisor handle a request like this directly, she talks to him before involving the manager. The entry is then made and marked as late under the utility's procedure. The conversation protects the record and the relationship at the same time. ### Habits for the first weeks - Meet with your manager and agree on the limits of your authority, what to report and how often. - Talk with each crew member one at a time about expectations. - Delegate on purpose, and record what was delegated and when you will check. - Keep a short log of your own decisions. It helps you learn and protects you later. - Ask for training in supervision. Technical certification alone does not teach leadership, and giving feedback is a skill worth practising early. The same expectations that you set for the crew apply to you: arrive on time, keep accurate records, follow procedures and own your mistakes. Crews watch what a new supervisor does far more closely than they listen to what the supervisor says, so a visible habit such as signing records only after checking them teaches more than any speech. When you are unsure whether a decision is yours to make, say so, find out and tell the crew what you learned. That honesty builds the trust that authority alone cannot.

checks.prompt: Which statement best describes the main change in a person's daily work when an operator becomes a supervisor?
choices: The focus stays on hands-on tasks while the title and pay change
The focus moves from daily operations to setting rates and approving the capital budget
The focus moves from doing each task to assigning, guiding and recording
The focus moves from the group's results to the supervisor's own personal skill with the equipment
checks.explanation: A supervisor is judged by what the group gets done safely and correctly, so the work shifts from doing to assigning, guiding, monitoring and documenting. The "The focus stays on hands-on tasks while the title and pay change" choice treats the new role as the old job with a new label, which leaves the supervising duties undone. The "The focus moves from daily operations to setting rates and approving the capital budget" choice describes decisions that sit well above a shift supervisor's authority, made by senior managers, a board or a council. The "The focus moves from the group's results to the supervisor's own personal skill with the equipment" choice mistakes the promotion for a technical reward, when the job is now measured by the group's results.

checks.prompt: At fictional Cedar Flats, a former crew mate asks new supervisor Marisol to leave a late entry out of the log because the crew has always done it that way. The best response is to:
choices: Explain privately that the log must match events and the rule applies to everyone
Refuse and stop speaking to him outside work so nobody thinks she is playing favourites
Agree this one time and fix the log herself later so the friendship is not damaged
Report him to the manager at once without first talking to him
checks.explanation: Consistency means one standard for every crew member, delivered in a friendly but clear private conversation. The "Refuse and stop speaking to him outside work so nobody thinks she is playing favourites" choice overcorrects, because consistency does not require coldness or cutting off a colleague. The "Agree this one time and fix the log herself later so the friendship is not damaged" choice creates a hidden exception and a false record, which is favouritism dressed as kindness. The "Report him to the manager at once without first talking to him" choice skips the direct conversation that protects the record and the working relationship.

checks.prompt: On an organisation chart, a supervisor usually sits:
choices: Above the manager, because the supervisor is closest to daily operations
Above the operators and below a manager, answering both ways
Beside the operators as another member of the crew with no added accountability
Outside the chart, because supervisors hold informal authority alone
checks.explanation: The supervisor is the middle link, answerable to the manager above and to the crew below. The "Above the manager, because the supervisor is closest to daily operations" choice reverses the usual order of reporting. The "Beside the operators as another member of the crew with no added accountability" choice ignores that the supervisor is accountable for the group's work. The "Outside the chart, because supervisors hold informal authority alone" choice confuses the supervisor with a lead operator, whose authority is often informal.

checks.prompt: Which decision is most likely to fall within a supervisor's usual authority?
choices: Changing the conditions written into the utility's operating permit
Setting the utility's customer water rates
Approving the capital budget for a new treatment plant

checks.explanation: Assigning work and scheduling within policy are the everyday powers of a supervisor. Hiring, firing and pay authority vary, so ask for the limits in writing. The "Changing the conditions written into the utility's operating permit" choice is set by the regulator and the permit process, not by a supervisor. The "Setting the utility's customer water rates" choice is decided by the body or official authorised to set rates, not a shift supervisor. The "Approving the capital budget for a new treatment plant" choice is a manager and board decision that sits well above a supervisor's role.

checks.prompt: A fictional supervisor's 40-hour week includes 14 hours of planning, meetings and records. What percent of the week is that, to one decimal place?
choices: 35.0 percent
14.0 percent
65.0 percent
285.7 percent
checks.explanation: Percent = part / whole x 100 = 14 hours / 40 hours x 100 = 35.0 percent. The "14.0 percent" choice reads the number of hours as a percent without dividing by the 40-hour week. The "65.0 percent" choice is the share of the week left over, 26 of 40 hours, not the share asked for. The "285.7 percent" choice divided the week by the 14 hours instead of the 14 hours by the week.

checks.prompt: Which description best fits a lead operator as the role is commonly used?
choices: Works hands-on and guides peers on technical tasks, often without formal disciplinary authority
Evaluates performance, writes reviews and starts discipline as a core duty
Plans the annual budget and reports to the governing board
Works alone and has no responsibility for how other operators work
checks.explanation: Titles vary, so compare duties: a lead operator guides while still doing the technical work. The "Evaluates performance, writes reviews and starts discipline as a core duty" choice describes a supervisor, whose authority over people is formal. The "Plans the annual budget and reports to the governing board" choice describes a manager, not a lead operator. The "Works alone and has no responsibility for how other operators work" choice ignores that a lead operator guides the work of peers.

modules.lesson: ### The supervisor's job in one sentence A supervisor guides the group toward its goals and sees that each member is productive. The second half matters: seeing that everyone is productive does not mean doing their work, and it does not mean ignoring the one person who is struggling. It means knowing what each person is assigned, checking that it was done correctly, and acting early when it was not. In a water or wastewater utility, the goals have a built-in public purpose. The crew exists to deliver safe water or to return treated wastewater to the environment, and routine tasks such as rounds, calibrations and sampling are the evidence that the purpose is being met. When a supervisor treats those tasks as paperwork, the evidence becomes unreliable and so does the safety margin behind it. ### Responsibility and accountability are different Responsibility is the duty to carry out a task. Accountability is answering for the result. A supervisor can hand responsibility for a task to an operator, but the supervisor stays accountable for the assignment: whether the person was trained, whether the instructions were clear, whether the check happened and whether the record is true. That is why delegating does not end with the handover. It ends with a check. Accountability also runs upward. If the manager asks why a monthly inspection was missed, "the operator forgot" is only a partial answer. A complete answer explains how the schedule was set, why the miss was not noticed and what has changed so it is noticed next time. ### Documentation and checklists as accountability tools Records and checklists do three jobs. They remind people of the steps, they show what was done and when, and they let someone else judge the work later. For a supervisor they are the main way to see what happened on a shift you were not standing next to. A useful loop has four parts, shown above. Assign the task with a clear checklist. The operator does the task and signs. The supervisor reviews the record, comparing it with what the process data, the equipment and the operator's description say. If there is a gap, correct it and note the correction, then use what you learned in the next assignment. A record that nobody reviews turns into a ritual, and a ritual is easy to fake. Review does not have to be slow: a two-minute look at the day's entries, with one spot check against the equipment or process data, is enough to show the crew that records matter. Good checklists are short enough to be completed honestly, written in the order the work is done, and updated when the procedure changes. A forty-line checklist that people tick in bulk at the end of the shift is worse than a ten-line one that is ticked as work is done. If a step is routinely skipped because it makes no sense, get the step reviewed and changed through the approved process rather than tolerating the skipping, and keep every check that the rules or permit require. ### A signature is a statement When someone signs or initials a task, they are stating that the task was done as described. Other people then rely on that statement: the next shift, the manager, an inspector, perhaps a court. A signature on a task that was not performed is a false record. It can mislead decisions, damage trust and, in a regulated job, put a certificate and a career at risk. Supervisors protect the principle in three ways. They never sign for work they have not checked. They make it easy to be honest, so that an operator can write "not done, pump out of service" without being blamed for the pump. And they respond fairly and consistently when a false entry is found: find out what happened, correct the record through the proper method rather than deleting it, and deal with the behaviour under the utility's policy. A supervisor who signs a review for tasks that were never inspected becomes part of the problem. ### Decisions made on shift Shift decisions are real decisions: postponing a task because the crew is short, accepting a reading that looks odd, sending a person home, or choosing between two urgent jobs. The supervisor owns the decisions made under their direction, including a decision to wait. Good habits are to note the decision, the reason and who was told. Others may need to defend the decision later, perhaps months afterwards, when memory has faded and the circumstances have changed, so the note should give enough context for a stranger to follow it. A short entry such as "Postponed valve exercising until Thursday, two operators out, manager informed at 10:15" protects the supervisor and gives the next shift the facts. If a decision is beyond your authority, escalate. If there is a risk to health or safety, protect people first and follow facility procedures; this course teaches recognition and purpose, not procedures. ### Certification and the idea of responsible charge Most states and provinces classify treatment plants and distribution or collection systems by size and complexity, and they certify operators by class. Many also require that a certified person be designated for a facility, often called the operator in responsible charge or a similar name. The concept is that one qualified person is answerable for operating decisions, for the actions of the staff under that role, and for meeting the rules. Failures to perform those duties can have personal consequences, such as action against the person's certificate. The details differ in every jurisdiction: the names of the classes, the experience and education required, the coverage a facility must provide and what happens if a certified person is absent. This course does not give tables. Check your state's or province's rules, and ask the certifying body when the answer affects a schedule. A supervisor who builds a shift roster should know which certificate class the facility needs on each shift and who holds it. ### Why the stakes are public Treatment and distribution protect people from waterborne disease. Bacteria, viruses and protozoa from human or animal waste can travel through drinking water, and a lapse in disinfection, pressure or cross-connection control can expose many customers at once. Some organisms reach people by a different route: Legionella, for example, can grow in warm water in building plumbing and is spread by breathing in fine mist rather than by drinking, which is why it is often called water-associated. In wastewater, operators and the public can also be exposed to pathogens, so the same discipline applies to handling and records. A supervisor does not need to be a microbiologist, but needs to understand that skipped checks and false records shorten the distance between a small error and a public-health problem. ### Worked example: covering a shift roster Harlow Creek is a fictional plant that needs one certified operator on site for 16 hours a day, 5 days a week. Each full-time operator is paid for 40 hours, but the supervisor plans on 10 percent of paid hours going to leave, sick time and training. Step 1: hours to cover = 16 hours per day x 5 days per week = 80 hours per week. Step 2: productive hours per operator = 40 hours x (1 - 0.10) = 36 hours per week. Step 3: operators needed = 80 / 36 = 2.22 full-time equivalents. If the plant staffs with full-time positions, round up to 3 operators: 2 operators give 2 x 36 = 72 available hours, about 8 hours short each week. Part-time relief is another way to cover the fraction. The supervisor then records the assumption and the leave allowance used, checks that the roster covers every required hour with a person who holds the certificate class the facility needs (check your state's or province's rules), and tells the manager that two operators would leave the plant short every week, before any extra absence. That note is the documentation loop in action.

checks.prompt: Which sentence best states the supervisor's job?
choices: Keep the crew busy at any task so nobody looks idle
Pass questions upward and wait for a manager's instructions
Guide the group toward its goals and see that each member is productive
Complete the hardest tasks personally so the crew has less to do
checks.explanation: Guiding and checking productivity are the heart of the role, and they apply to each member, including a struggling one. The "Keep the crew busy at any task so nobody looks idle" choice confuses activity with productive work toward the goals. The "Pass questions upward and wait for a manager's instructions" choice gives the crew no direction of its own. The "Complete the hardest tasks personally so the crew has less to do" choice replaces supervising with doing.

checks.prompt: Which statement best separates responsibility from accountability?
choices: They mean the same thing, so handing off a task also hands off the answer
Responsibility is answering for the result; accountability is the duty to do a task
Responsibility is the duty to do a task; accountability is answering for the result
Responsibility belongs to managers and accountability belongs to operators
checks.explanation: A supervisor can hand over responsibility for a task but remains accountable for training, clear instructions, checking and the true record. The "They mean the same thing, so handing off a task also hands off the answer" choice ignores that the supervisor stays accountable for the assignment. The "Responsibility is answering for the result; accountability is the duty to do a task" choice reverses the two terms. The "Responsibility belongs to managers and accountability belongs to operators" choice assigns the terms by job title instead of by meaning.

checks.prompt: An operator signs a checklist line saying a chlorine pump was inspected, but the inspection did not happen. Why is this serious?
choices: It matters just to the operator, because nobody else reads the log or the checklist after the shift
Others rely on the signature, and a false one can carry personal consequences
It is serious if a regulator finds it first, and the entry is harmless otherwise
It is not serious if the pump ran normally that day, because the outcome looks the same
checks.explanation: The signature is a statement of fact. A false one misleads decisions and can put a certificate and a career at risk. The "It matters just to the operator, because nobody else reads the log or the checklist after the shift" choice ignores that the next shift, the manager and inspectors depend on the record. The "It is serious if a regulator finds it first, and the entry is harmless otherwise" choice treats honesty as a matter of getting caught. The "It is not serious if the pump ran normally that day, because the outcome looks the same" choice treats the record as paperwork, when the signature is a statement others rely on.

checks.prompt: A daily checklist lists 18 tasks. At the end of the shift 15 are signed. What percent of the tasks remain unsigned, to one decimal place?
choices: 20.0 percent
3.0 percent
83.3 percent
16.7 percent
checks.explanation: Unsigned = 18 - 15 = 3 tasks, and 3 / 18 x 100 = 16.7 percent. The "20.0 percent" choice divided the unsigned tasks by the signed tasks instead of by the full list. The "3.0 percent" choice used the count of unsigned tasks as a percent without dividing by 18. The "83.3 percent" choice is the signed share, not the unsigned share.

checks.prompt: Which statement best describes the idea of an operator in responsible charge?
choices: The role carries authority but brings no personal consequences if the duties are not performed
A certified person named as answerable for operations and staff supervision; local rules set details
The role is identical across jurisdictions, so no rules need to be checked by the supervisor
Any operator on shift is in charge by default, whatever certificate they hold or the rules require
checks.explanation: Treat it as a concept and check your state's or province's rules for the actual requirements. The "The role carries authority but brings no personal consequences if the duties are not performed" choice ignores that failing in the duties can lead to action against the person's certificate. The "The role is identical across jurisdictions, so no rules need to be checked by the supervisor" choice overlooks that classes, names and coverage rules differ between jurisdictions. The "Any operator on shift is in charge by default, whatever certificate they hold or the rules require" choice ignores that the rules name who holds the role and what certificate it requires.

checks.prompt: A supervisor postpones a routine valve check because two operators are out. Which entry best protects everyone?
choices: Valve check was completed and signed off as normal for the shift
Valve check was not completed on this shift
Crew was too lazy to finish the valve check on the day shift
Valve check moved to Thursday, two operators out, manager told
checks.explanation: A shift decision should note what was decided, why and who was informed. The "Valve check was completed and signed off as normal for the shift" choice is a false entry, which misleads anyone relying on the record. The "Valve check was not completed on this shift" choice gives no reason, no new date and no record of who was told. The "Crew was too lazy to finish the valve check on the day shift" choice blames people instead of recording the decision and its reason.

modules.evidence:
### Fictional scenario: the Pinecrest flushing program

Pinecrest Regional Water is a fictional utility with 45 operators. It is starting a new hydrant flushing program that needs a written checklist and weekly records. Three supervisors react differently: one writes the plan alone and checks every crew, one tells the crew to handle it, and one asks the crews to draft the checklist first. The manager wants a span of control of 9 for every supervisor, but a review says the work is complex enough to consider a span of 6.

### Your decision

Decide which style fits which crew and how many supervisors each span would need.
modules.assignment: Write a one-page comparison of how each of the five styles would introduce the flushing program, including training, checklists and accountability, and recommend a style for a new crew and for an experienced crew. Calculate the supervisors needed for a span of 9 and for a span of 6, and say in two sentences what the utility gains and pays for by narrowing the span.
rubric: Describes each style accurately, including how the bureaucratic style relies on the written rule.
Gives an advantage and a disadvantage for each style in the flushing context.
Calculates 45 / 9 = 5 supervisors and 45 / 6 = 7.5, rounded up to 8.
Recommends matching the style to the crew and the situation and explains why.
modules.facilitatorGuide: Span 9: 45 / 9 = 5 supervisors. Span 6: 45 / 6 = 7.5, so 8 supervisors, which is 3 more. Accept answers that note the extra cost buys closer oversight and that the right span depends on the risk and complexity of the work, with no single number correct. Look for a directive style for the new crew, democratic input for the experienced crew and bureaucratic discipline for regulated records. Do not accept a fixed span of control as a rule for all utilities.

modules.lesson: ### Five styles in plain terms A management style is the habitual way a leader makes decisions and gets work done. Textbooks describe five that come up often in utilities. No one fits a single label all the time, but most supervisors lean toward one. - **Autocratic.** The leader decides and tells. Directions are specific, questions are few and the leader checks closely. - **Paternalistic.** The leader still decides, but acts as a protective parent figure: explains decisions in terms of the crew's best interest, looks after people and expects loyalty in return. - **Democratic.** The leader brings the group into the decision. Views are asked for and weighed, and the group often owns the outcome, while the leader keeps the final responsibility. - **Laissez-faire.** The leader sets a goal and steps back. People choose their methods and timing with little direction or follow-up. - **Bureaucratic.** The rulebook leads. Procedures, forms and approvals decide what happens, and the leader makes sure the rules are followed. The first four sit along a line from the leader keeping control to staff using their own judgement. Autocratic and paternalistic leaders both keep the decision; the paternalistic leader explains it and protects people. Laissez-faire leaves the method to each person rather than to a group vote. Bureaucratic is different because it does not depend on who decides; it depends on the written rule. A bureaucratic leader can be strict or relaxed, but always points to the procedure. ### The same task under each style: a filter check To see the styles in action, imagine that the fictional Birchwood Plant needs a weekly check of filter performance, including a look at the run records, the backwash and the media surface. The supervisor needs a new operator, Imani, to start doing it. - **Autocratic:** The supervisor shows Imani exactly what to do, in order, and tells her to follow it. Imani reports to the supervisor after each check, and the supervisor inspects the filter personally to confirm. Accountability is clear but initiative is low. - **Paternalistic:** The supervisor walks Imani through the check, explains that it protects the people who drink the water, and promises to cover for her while she learns. The supervisor decides the schedule and expects Imani to be grateful. Training is warm but decisions stay with the supervisor. - **Democratic:** The supervisor asks Imani and two colleagues how the check should be done, sends their suggested checklist changes through the plant's document approval and shares the results at a team meeting. Ownership is high, but agreement takes time. - **Laissez-faire:** The supervisor says, "The filters need checking weekly. Handle it." Experienced operators may do well; Imani may not know what good looks like, and nobody is likely to notice if the check slips. - **Bureaucratic:** The supervisor gives Imani the approved procedure and form, requires a signature on each step and files the form. Consistency is high, but a new problem that the form does not cover may go unnoticed. Each version handles training, checklists and accountability in a different way, and each has a failure mode. ### Advantages and disadvantages - **Autocratic** is fast and clear, which suits new crews and time-pressured decisions. Disadvantages: weaker morale, little learning, and quality that depends on the supervisor being present. - **Paternalistic** builds loyalty and protects people. Disadvantages: staff can become dependent, and criticism may feel like betrayal. - **Democratic** draws on the crew's knowledge and builds ownership. Disadvantages: slow, and who decides and who follows up can blur unless the supervisor assigns them; the supervisor stays accountable either way. - **Laissez-faire** gives skilled staff freedom and encourages initiative. Disadvantages: goals drift, weak performers are not noticed and the supervisor may seem absent. - **Bureaucratic** gives consistency and an audit trail. Disadvantages: rigid, slow to adapt and prone to ticking boxes. ### Choosing a style for the situation Good supervisors adjust. Start from the people and the situation, not from your preference. - A new crew, an unfamiliar process or an urgent decision with no time to consult leans toward directive, autocratic behaviour for that moment, ideally with an explanation afterwards. - A skilled, stable crew improving a routine, such as a flushing schedule, benefits from democratic input. - Highly experienced specialists on a well-defined project can work with laissez-faire freedom, as long as there are clear goals and check-in points. - Regulated tasks with fixed forms and approvals need bureaucratic discipline, whatever the leader's temperament. - A crew that is struggling or grieving may need the care of a paternalistic approach, provided it does not turn into over-protection. The risk of staying in one style is that the crew only ever gets one kind of leader. Notice which style you default to under stress and decide on purpose when to switch. ### Organisation charts and span of control An organisation chart shows who reports to whom. Charts differ by utility. Organisations with autocratic or paternalistic cultures often have many layers, so decisions travel up and down a long chain. Organisations that use laissez-faire or highly democratic styles are often flatter, with fewer layers and more people per supervisor. Span of control is the number of people who report directly to one supervisor or manager. A narrow span allows closer supervision but may need more supervisors or more layers. A wide span may need fewer supervisory posts and gives people more freedom, but leaves the supervisor less time to coach each person. The right span depends on how complex and risky the work is, how experienced the crew is, and whether the staff work in one place or across a wide area. No single number is correct. ### Worked example: span of control A fictional utility, Pinecrest Regional Water, has 45 operators and wants each supervisor to have a span of 9. Step 1: supervisors needed = 45 operators / 9 per supervisor = 5 supervisors. Step 2: if the five supervisors report directly to the manager, the manager's own span is 5, so for span reasons this structure needs no extra layer between the manager and the supervisors. Step 3: if the span were cut to 6 because the work is more complex, supervisors needed = 45 / 6 = 7.5, so 8 supervisors, for example seven teams of 6 and one of 3 (7 x 6 + 3 = 45). The example shows the trade-off. Narrowing the span from 9 to 6 adds three supervisors, and the utility pays for closer oversight. Whether that is worth it depends on the risk of the work. ### A mixed-style day Joaquin supervises a fictional Pinecrest crew of six. At 7:00 a main break forces a quick reassignment of the whole team, so he tells people where to go and what to do, and takes questions afterwards: autocratic for ten minutes because time is short. At 10:00 he asks the crew how to reorder the repair backlog, listens to the experienced operators and decides together with them: democratic, because their knowledge improves the plan. At 14:00 a sampling form must be completed exactly as the approved procedure says, so he asks to see each signed step: bureaucratic, because the approved procedure must be followed exactly and the record must show it. Nobody thinks he is inconsistent, because he explained why the approach changed. Switching styles to fit the moment is a skill; switching without explanation, or favouring one person's input, is what erodes trust. ### Putting it together Notice which style the situation calls for, match the way you use it to the crew in front of you, and check the result. The structure of the organisation then makes the style easier or harder to use: a supervisor with a span of 12 may struggle to coach each person weekly, and a decision that must climb a seven-layer chain may be slow.

checks.prompt: At fictional Birchwood Plant a supervisor tells a new operator, "The filters need checking weekly; handle it," and does not follow up. Which management style does this show?
choices: Autocratic
Laissez-faire
Bureaucratic
Paternalistic
checks.explanation: Setting a goal and stepping back is laissez-faire. It suits skilled staff, but a new operator may not know what good looks like and a missed check may go unnoticed. The "Autocratic" choice would mean detailed instructions and close checking, which are missing here. The "Bureaucratic" choice would involve an approved procedure and form, which are not mentioned. The "Paternalistic" choice would involve the supervisor explaining the decision, protecting the operator and expecting loyalty, none of which appear here.

checks.prompt: A supervisor decides the crew's schedule, explains that it protects their families and expects loyalty in return. Which style is this?
choices: Laissez-faire
Autocratic
Paternalistic
Democratic
checks.explanation: Paternalistic leaders decide, act like a protective parent and expect loyalty. The risk is dependence and difficulty with criticism. The "Laissez-faire" choice would leave people to choose their own methods and timing. The "Autocratic" choice is close, but the caring explanation and expected loyalty point to the paternalistic style. The "Democratic" choice would involve asking the crew for views before deciding.

checks.prompt: What is the main drawback of the democratic style?
choices: It removes the supervisor's final responsibility for the outcome
It can be slow, and roles can blur unless assigned
It gives staff no voice in the decisions that affect their work
It depends on strict written procedures and approval forms
checks.explanation: Democratic input improves ownership and uses the crew's knowledge, but takes time, and the supervisor still answers for the outcome. The "It removes the supervisor's final responsibility for the outcome" choice is false, since the leader keeps the final responsibility. The "It gives staff no voice in the decisions that affect their work" choice describes the autocratic style, the opposite of democratic. The "It depends on strict written procedures and approval forms" choice describes the bureaucratic style.

checks.prompt: Which situation most clearly calls for a directive approach for the moment?
choices: A skilled crew is reviewing a flushing schedule with weeks to spare
A routine form must be completed exactly each week
A specialist team has a clear goal and years of experience
A new crew must act quickly on an unfamiliar process and there is no time to consult
checks.explanation: Match the style to the people and the situation; directing suits urgent decisions and new crews, ideally with an explanation afterwards. The "A skilled crew is reviewing a flushing schedule with weeks to spare" choice favours democratic input because there is time and knowledge to draw on. The "A routine form must be completed exactly each week" choice points to bureaucratic discipline rather than directing the crew in the moment. The "A specialist team has a clear goal and years of experience" choice suits more freedom with check-in points.

checks.prompt: A fictional utility has 24 operators and 4 supervisors, and every operator reports to one of the supervisors. What is the average span of control per supervisor?
choices: 96 operators
0.2 operators
28 operators
6 operators
checks.explanation: Span of control = people reporting / supervisors = 24 / 4 = 6. The "96 operators" choice multiplied the two numbers instead of dividing. The "0.2 operators" choice divided the supervisors by the operators (4 / 24 = 0.17, shown as 0.2), which gives supervisors per operator, the inverted ratio. The "28 operators" choice added the supervisors to the operators instead of dividing.

checks.prompt: Which statement about organisation charts is most accurate?
choices: One chart shape suits any utility, so each should copy the same layout
Charts differ; autocratic cultures tend to be layered and laissez-faire ones flatter
Extra layers speed decisions because more people approve each one on the way up
A flat chart has more layers than a tall chart, with fewer people for each supervisor
checks.explanation: Charts reflect the utility's size and culture. More layers lengthen the path of decisions; flatter charts widen the span of control. The "One chart shape suits any utility, so each should copy the same layout" choice ignores differences in size, risk and culture. The "Extra layers speed decisions because more people approve each one on the way up" choice misses that more layers usually slow decisions. The "A flat chart has more layers than a tall chart, with fewer people for each supervisor" choice reverses the meaning of flat.
