modules.lesson: ### Setting expectations Many performance problems begin with an expectation that was never stated, or was stated once and then not followed up. A supervisor leading a group through a change, such as a new procedure, a new piece of equipment or a changed schedule, should state four things in plain words: what is changing, why, what is expected of each person and by when, and how progress will be checked. Say it face to face, then confirm it in writing so everyone works from the same version. A good expectation is specific and observable. "Do a better job on logs" is vague. "Complete each log entry before leaving the area and record the reading as measured, in the units and precision the procedure requires" can be checked. People can only meet expectations they understand, so ask them to say back what they will do. A thirty-second check can save weeks of confusion. ### Why people resist change When a procedure or schedule changes, resistance is normal and often useful. People worry about losing skill, status or time, and sometimes they spot a real flaw in the plan. A supervisor who treats every objection as insubordination loses the information. Listen first, separate fear from fact, and answer the factual points honestly. If a concern is valid, take it to the manager and tell the crew what happened to it. If it is not, explain why the change goes ahead anyway. Early and honest communication about what is known and unknown prevents rumours from filling the gap. ### Delegating without letting go Delegation means giving someone the responsibility to carry out a task while you keep accountability. It is how a supervisor finds time for supervising, and it is how operators grow. A sound delegation names the task, the result wanted, the limits of authority, the deadline and the point at which the supervisor will check. Match the task to the person's skill and training, and do not delegate something that needs your authority, such as a disciplinary decision. Common mistakes are to delegate and then hover, to delegate only the dull jobs, and to delegate with no check and then blame the person for the result. A better pattern is to start with a smaller step and a close check, then widen the scope as the person shows reliability. Record what you delegated and when you will review it. ### Coaching and directing Directing tells someone what to do and how. It works for new tasks, unsafe habits and short deadlines. Coaching asks questions and helps the person work out the answer, which builds judgement. It works for people who have the basic skills and need to improve. Most supervisors use both: direct when the person lacks the skill or the time is short, coach when the person has the skill and the aim is growth. A coaching conversation can follow four steps. Describe what you observed, without judgement. Ask the person how they saw it. Agree on what to try next. Set a time to look again. Feedback works best when it is prompt, specific and about the work, not the person. Praise is feedback too: tell people what they did well, so they repeat it. ### Handling a poor performer fairly A poor performer is a person whose work does not meet the agreed standard. For a routine performance issue, fairness has a clear order. If the work creates an immediate hazard, deal with the hazard first under facility procedures. 1. Check the facts. Was the standard clear, was training provided and was the equipment working? Some "poor performance" is a training or equipment gap. 2. Talk privately and promptly. Describe the gap, the effect on the crew or the public, and the expectation. Listen to the explanation. 3. Agree on support and a time frame, such as a refresher, a closer check or a shadowing period. 4. Record the conversation, the agreement and the follow-up date, and give the person a copy. 5. Follow up as promised. If the work improves, say so. If it does not, involve the manager or human resources and follow the utility's discipline process and any labour agreement. Treat the person the same way you would treat any other member of the crew, and do not discuss their performance with the rest of the crew. Do not skip steps because you are frustrated, and do not use a formal process as a surprise. The aim is a person who meets the standard, and the record shows you worked toward it fairly. ### Documenting events Write down significant events while memory is fresh: what happened, when, who was involved, what was observed, what was done and who was told. Stay with facts and quotes, and leave out opinions and guesses. A note such as "Operator arrived 25 minutes after the start of shift; said bus was late; reminded of the call-in rule" is useful. A note such as "Operator is lazy" is not. Keep records in the place and format the utility requires, protect private information and make sure the same standards apply to everyone. Good records protect the supervisor, the employee and the utility, and they also show patterns that one event cannot. ### Team troubleshooting and escalation When something goes wrong, such as a repeated sampling error or a pump that keeps tripping, a team approach usually finds causes faster than one person. State the problem in a sentence. Collect the facts: what changed, when it began and what the records show. List possible causes without judging them. Test the likeliest cause in the safest, simplest way. Agree on who does what and when you will meet again. Record what you tried, including what did not work. Escalation is part of the process, not a failure. The flow above puts safety first, then authority. If a problem puts people or the public at risk, protect people and tell the manager now, following facility procedures. If it is within your authority, decide, act and document. If it is beyond your authority, escalate with the facts and the time, and keep a record either way. This course gives recognition and purpose only; your facility's procedures set the steps. ### Worked example: the operator-to-supervisor transition Tariq Hassan has been promoted to supervisor of a fictional six-person crew at Willow Bend Utility. His first month tells a common story. He keeps doing the weekly equipment rounds himself, 6 tasks of 45 minutes each, because he does them quickly. The crew sees little direction, and one operator, Lena, begins missing logs. Step 1: Tariq's time spent on the rounds = 6 x 45 minutes = 270 minutes, or 4.5 hours per week. Step 2: he decides to delegate 4 of the 6 tasks, which frees 4 x 45 = 180 minutes, or 3 hours per week. Step 3: he agrees with the crew who does which task, states the expectation in writing and sets a check at the end of the week. Step 4: about Lena, he checks the facts first and finds she was never shown the new log format. He trains her, records the conversation and follows up in a week. Her logs improve. In six weeks Tariq reports that he spends his freed 3 hours on coaching and records. He still does a couple of tasks, because staying in touch with the work keeps his judgement sharp, but he no longer fills the day with them. His crew now knows what to expect and who decides what, and when a pump trips he knows whether to troubleshoot with the team, decide or escalate.

checks.prompt: Which expectation is specific and observable?
choices: Take more pride in the paperwork and show the care that the job needs
Try to be more careful with the log entries over the coming weeks
Log each reading as measured, before leaving the area
Do a better job on the logs this month and keep the entries tidy
checks.explanation: A good expectation can be seen and checked, and people can say back what they will do. The "Take more pride in the paperwork and show the care that the job needs" choice describes an attitude and not an action. The "Try to be more careful with the log entries over the coming weeks" choice sets no checkable behaviour. The "Do a better job on the logs this month and keep the entries tidy" choice is vague and cannot be checked.

checks.prompt: A supervisor delegates a weekly inspection to an operator. Who remains accountable for the assignment?
choices: The supervisor, who trains, instructs and checks the work
The operator alone, since the whole task and its result were handed over
The manager, because supervisors are not allowed to delegate any task
Nobody in particular, because the task is now routine and well understood
checks.explanation: Delegation hands over responsibility, and it ends with a check. The "The operator alone, since the whole task and its result were handed over" choice ignores that delegating transfers the task, not the accountability. The "The manager, because supervisors are not allowed to delegate any task" choice wrongly says that supervisors cannot delegate. The "Nobody in particular, because the task is now routine and well understood" choice confuses routine with unowned.

checks.prompt: An experienced operator keeps making the same small error in a routine task. Which approach best builds judgement?
choices: Mention it in front of the whole crew so the others learn from it
Tell the operator to follow the procedure and then leave the matter alone
Describe what was seen, ask the operator's view, agree on a next step
Wait and see whether the error fades away without any feedback given
checks.explanation: Coaching suits people who have the skill and need to improve; direct when the skill or time is missing. The "Mention it in front of the whole crew so the others learn from it" choice damages trust and is not private, specific feedback. The "Tell the operator to follow the procedure and then leave the matter alone" choice directs without learning why the error is happening. The "Wait and see whether the error fades away without any feedback given" choice gives no feedback and loses time.

checks.prompt: What should a supervisor do first when a crew member's work falls short of the standard and there is no immediate hazard?
choices: Wait for a few more mistakes before taking any action with the person
Start the formal discipline process at once, before looking at the cause
Warn the whole crew about the problem so that nobody repeats it
Check whether the standard, training and equipment were in place
checks.explanation: Some poor performance comes from training or equipment gaps, so fairness starts with the facts. The "Wait for a few more mistakes before taking any action with the person" choice delays feedback and lets the problem grow. The "Start the formal discipline process at once, before looking at the cause" choice jumps ahead before knowing the cause. The "Warn the whole crew about the problem so that nobody repeats it" choice does not address the person fairly or privately.

checks.prompt: Which note about a late arrival is best?
choices: Arrived 25 minutes late; said bus delayed; reminded of call-in rule
Operator is lazy and keeps coming in late whenever he feels like it
Late arrival was noticed this morning on the day shift
Operator came in late again, no excuse offered, so the pattern continues
checks.explanation: Good records state facts, quotes and actions, and leave out opinions and guesses. The "Operator is lazy and keeps coming in late whenever he feels like it" choice states an opinion and a sweeping claim, not facts. The "Late arrival was noticed this morning on the day shift" choice gives only a rough time, does not say how late and records no action. The "Operator came in late again, no excuse offered, so the pattern continues" choice claims a pattern with no dates, does not say how late and records no action by the supervisor.

checks.prompt: In a fictional crew, 7 of 28 logs from the past month were submitted late. What percent were late?
choices: 25.0 percent
21.0 percent
75.0 percent
4.0 percent
checks.explanation: Percent = 7 / 28 x 100 = 25.0 percent. The "21.0 percent" choice subtracted 7 from 28 and used the result as a percent. The "75.0 percent" choice is the percent submitted on time, not late. The "4.0 percent" choice divided the total by the late logs (28 / 7 = 4) and labelled that ratio a percent.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility gives Tomas the title senior supervisor, but he cannot assign work, change schedules or recommend discipline. Which statement best reflects how supervisor status is usually judged?
choices: Status is identical across states and provinces, so no checking of local rules is needed
Status depends on how long the person has worked at the utility and their seniority
A job title is the legal definition, so the title decides whether he is a supervisor
Real authority over the work and people matters more than the title
finalAssessment.explanation: The dictionary meaning is a person who oversees others, and the legal tests usually look at real authority. Check the rules that apply to your employer. The "Status is identical across states and provinces, so no checking of local rules is needed" choice ignores that legal tests differ between jurisdictions and laws. The "Status depends on how long the person has worked at the utility and their seniority" choice confuses seniority with authority over other workers. The "A job title is the legal definition, so the title decides whether he is a supervisor" choice assumes a title carries authority that the person does not actually have.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant must have one operator on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Each operator is paid for 40 hours a week, and planning assumes 15 percent of paid hours go to leave and training. How many operators are needed, rounded up to a whole person?
choices: 5 operators
4 operators
7 operators
6 operators
finalAssessment.explanation: Hours to cover = 24 x 7 = 168. Productive hours each = 40 x 0.85 = 34. Operators = 168 / 34 = 4.94, rounded up to 5. The "4 operators" choice ignores the leave allowance and rounds down, leaving some hours uncovered. The "7 operators" choice divided the 168 weekly hours by the 24 hours in a day. The "6 operators" choice applied the 15 percent allowance twice.

finalAssessment.prompt: Elena supervises three trainees learning a new chemical feed system under a tight commissioning date. Which approach best fits?
choices: Hold a vote among the trainees on how the new system should be run
Hand them the manual and sign each step later without watching the work
Direct and check closely now, explain why, and loosen control as skills grow
Leave the trainees to find their own methods because that is how they learn fastest
finalAssessment.explanation: New crews and urgent work lean toward directive leadership, adjusted as the people become competent. The "Hold a vote among the trainees on how the new system should be run" choice asks people without the knowledge to decide what they do not yet understand. The "Hand them the manual and sign each step later without watching the work" choice relies on paperwork and misses coaching in the field. The "Leave the trainees to find their own methods because that is how they learn fastest" choice suits experienced staff working within approved procedures, not trainees on a tight deadline.

finalAssessment.prompt: Operator Gus has missed three sampling rounds this month. Any required follow-up on the missed samples is under way. What is the best first step in addressing his performance?
choices: Discuss it with the rest of the crew to see what they think should happen
Issue a written warning today so that the record is clear from the very start
Wait until the end of the year to mention it in the review
Check the standard, training and equipment, then talk with Gus privately
finalAssessment.explanation: Fair handling starts with the facts, then a private talk, agreed support, a record and follow-up. The "Discuss it with the rest of the crew to see what they think should happen" choice breaks privacy and invites gossip. The "Issue a written warning today so that the record is clear from the very start" choice skips the check of whether the standard and training were in place. The "Wait until the end of the year to mention it in the review" choice delays feedback far beyond the time it can help.

finalAssessment.prompt: Dara spent 34 of her 40 paid hours on hands-on work as an operator. As a supervisor, still paid for 40 hours, she now spends 15 hours hands-on. What share of her week is hands-on now, to one decimal place?
choices: 44.1 percent
37.5 percent
62.5 percent
85.0 percent
finalAssessment.explanation: Share = 15 hours / 40 hours x 100 = 37.5 percent. Her hands-on share fell from 85 percent as the supervising tasks grew. The "44.1 percent" choice compares the new hours with her old hands-on hours instead of with the 40-hour week. The "62.5 percent" choice is the share of her week that is not hands-on, 25 of 40 hours. The "85.0 percent" choice is her share as an operator, before the promotion.

finalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor learns that an operator signed off a backwash inspection that a coworker says was skipped because the pump was down. The best action is to:
choices: Leave the entry alone because the shift is over and the pump was down anyway
Countersign the entry to show that the supervisor reviewed it, then move on
Hear the operator, check the facts, fix the record if wrong and apply policy
Delete the entry quietly so the log looks clean and the matter goes away
finalAssessment.explanation: Fair fact-finding, an honest correction and a consistent response protect the record and the person. The "Leave the entry alone because the shift is over and the pump was down anyway" choice leaves a possibly false record unresolved and teaches the crew that signatures are cheap. The "Countersign the entry to show that the supervisor reviewed it, then move on" choice puts a review signature on an entry nobody has verified, which others may read as confirmation. The "Delete the entry quietly so the log looks clean and the matter goes away" choice destroys the evidence and hides the problem.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility has 48 operators. The manager wants a span of control of 8 per supervisor. How many supervisors are needed?
choices: 8 supervisors
384 supervisors
40 supervisors
6 supervisors
finalAssessment.explanation: Supervisors = 48 / 8 = 6. The "8 supervisors" choice confused the span with the number of supervisors. The "384 supervisors" choice multiplied 48 by 8 instead of dividing. The "40 supervisors" choice subtracted 8 from 48 instead of dividing.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional supervisor does 8 weekly tasks of 30 minutes each and delegates 5 of them. Assuming 4 weeks in a month, how many hours per month does this free?
choices: 10.0 hours
16.0 hours
4.0 hours
2.5 hours
finalAssessment.explanation: Weekly saving = 5 x 30 = 150 minutes = 2.5 hours. Monthly = 2.5 x 4 = 10.0 hours. The "16.0 hours" choice used all 8 tasks instead of the 5 that were delegated. The "4.0 hours" choice is the weekly time for all 8 tasks, not the monthly saving from the 5 delegated. The "2.5 hours" choice is the weekly saving and was not multiplied by 4 weeks.

finalAssessment.prompt: A new supervisor's close friend on the crew has arrived late several times, and the supervisor overlooked it when they were peers. The best next step is to:
choices: Ask a different supervisor to handle the friend so the friendship is protected
Talk privately, restate the expectation, apply the same standard and record it
Announce a stricter attendance rule to the whole crew without naming anyone
Say nothing, since the friend knows the rule and the crew will understand
finalAssessment.explanation: Consistency and a private, documented conversation protect the standard and the relationship. The "Ask a different supervisor to handle the friend so the friendship is protected" choice hands off a duty that belongs to the supervisor just to protect the friendship. The "Announce a stricter attendance rule to the whole crew without naming anyone" choice burdens people who did nothing wrong and avoids the real conversation. The "Say nothing, since the friend knows the rule and the crew will understand" choice lets favouritism stand and teaches the crew that standards depend on friendship.

finalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor tells an operator to skip a routine check to save time, and an error follows. Who answers for the decision to skip?
choices: The operator, because the operator was the person who did the work on the shift
The manager, because supervisors have no authority over how routine checks are done
The supervisor owns the instruction; the operator should still raise concerns
Nobody, because routine shift decisions are not recorded and are hard to trace
finalAssessment.explanation: The supervisor owns decisions made under the supervisor's direction, which is why such decisions should be recorded with reasons. The "The operator, because the operator was the person who did the work on the shift" choice ignores that the supervisor made and owns the decision. The "The manager, because supervisors have no authority over how routine checks are done" choice denies the supervisor's authority over assignments on shift. The "Nobody, because routine shift decisions are not recorded and are hard to trace" choice treats the absence of a record as an absence of accountability.

finalAssessment.prompt: A fictional crew has an annual budget of $250,000, and the plan assigns 12 percent of it to overtime. How many dollars is the overtime allocation?
finalAssessment.explanation: Share = 250,000 x 0.12 = 30,000 dollars. The percent is an assumption in this question, not a standard. The "$3,000" choice moved the decimal point one place too far. The "$20,833" choice divided the budget by 12 instead of multiplying by 12 percent. The "$238,000" choice subtracted 12 thousand from the budget instead of taking a percentage.

finalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor notices an unexplained alarm pattern that may point to a risk to the public, and the manager is in a meeting. What is the best action?
choices: Decide that it is probably nothing and move on
Wait for the meeting to end so the manager is not disturbed
Protect people and follow facility procedures, and tell the manager now
Handle it quietly and tell the manager next week
finalAssessment.explanation: Safety and public health come first in the escalation flow; facility procedures set the steps. The "Decide that it is probably nothing and move on" choice guesses instead of acting on a possible risk. The "Wait for the meeting to end so the manager is not disturbed" choice delays notice of a possible risk. The "Handle it quietly and tell the manager next week" choice hides a problem that others need to know about.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which statement best separates a supervisor from a manager?
choices: A supervisor sets utility policy, while a manager carries out the daily tasks
A supervisor and a manager hold the same duties and differ in pay grade alone
A supervisor works the same hands-on hours as an operator, while a manager does not
A supervisor directs daily group work; a manager answers for budgets and plans
finalAssessment.explanation: Typically the supervisor works in shifts and weeks and the manager in months, budgets and plans, though the split varies by utility. The "A supervisor sets utility policy, while a manager carries out the daily tasks" choice reverses the roles. The "A supervisor and a manager hold the same duties and differ in pay grade alone" choice ignores the difference in time horizon and scope of the two roles. The "A supervisor works the same hands-on hours as an operator, while a manager does not" choice treats the difference as hours worked instead of duties.

finalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor is building a roster and is unsure which certificate class the facility needs on each shift. The best step is to:
choices: Check the certifying body's rules and ask the manager first
Post the roster and correct it if anyone complains
Use the class that was needed at the last job
Copy the roster used by a neighbouring utility
finalAssessment.explanation: Classification and coverage differ by state and province, so check your state's or province's rules. The "Post the roster and correct it if anyone complains" choice risks a shift without the needed certified person. The "Use the class that was needed at the last job" choice relies on memory of a different facility instead of the rule. The "Copy the roster used by a neighbouring utility" choice assumes another utility's classification and coverage apply to this facility.

finalAssessment.prompt: An experienced crew is revising the flushing schedule, and the supervisor has several weeks. Which approach best fits?
choices: Ask the crew for ideas, weigh them, then decide and own the plan
Write the schedule alone and announce it at the next crew meeting
Send the question to the manager to decide and wait for the answer
Tell the crew to sort it out among themselves and not report back
finalAssessment.explanation: A skilled crew, time and a routine improvement all favour democratic input, with the supervisor keeping final responsibility. The "Write the schedule alone and announce it at the next crew meeting" choice wastes the crew's field knowledge when time allows input. The "Send the question to the manager to decide and wait for the answer" choice passes up a decision that a supervisor can usually make, with any approval the utility requires. The "Tell the crew to sort it out among themselves and not report back" choice drops the supervisor's accountability for the outcome.

finalAssessment.prompt: A new procedure begins next week. Which communication best prepares the crew?
choices: Post the new procedure on the board without any comment or explanation
State what changes, why, who does what and how it is checked, in writing
Mention it briefly at the end of the shift while people are packing up to go home
Let each person find out from a coworker as the week goes on
finalAssessment.explanation: People can only meet expectations they understand, and a written statement of what, why, who and how it is checked gives everyone the same version; a say-back can then confirm it. The "Post the new procedure on the board without any comment or explanation" choice offers no explanation and invites mistakes. The "Mention it briefly at the end of the shift while people are packing up to go home" choice gives no detail, no reason and no way to confirm understanding. The "Let each person find out from a coworker as the week goes on" choice leaves the message to chance and rumour.

finalAssessment.prompt: In her first week Marisol notices a pump fault. She is tempted to repair it herself. Which action best fits the supervisor's role?
choices: Assign the repair to a qualified operator, check progress and record the outcome
Ask the manager to choose which operator should do the repair
Repair it herself so the job is done quickly and correctly
Wait to see whether anyone else notices the fault
finalAssessment.explanation: Assigning, checking and recording are the supervisor's duties. She can still help when the situation truly needs it. The "Ask the manager to choose which operator should do the repair" choice hands the manager a shift assignment that belongs to the supervisor. The "Repair it herself so the job is done quickly and correctly" choice keeps her in the operator role while the supervising work waits. The "Wait to see whether anyone else notices the fault" choice gives no direction and leaves the problem unowned.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which statement best explains why lapses in routine checks matter to the public?
choices: Pathogens spread through water when it looks cloudy and not when clear
Pathogens in water can reach many customers at once through one lapse
Checks are mostly paperwork and rarely affect anyone outside the utility itself
Public health is the regulator's concern, not the operators' daily concern
finalAssessment.explanation: Treatment and distribution are the barrier against waterborne disease, so skipped checks and false records shorten the distance between a small error and a public-health problem. The "Pathogens spread through water when it looks cloudy and not when clear" choice wrongly assumes contaminated water always looks different. The "Checks are mostly paperwork and rarely affect anyone outside the utility itself" choice treats the checks as formalities rather than evidence of safety. The "Public health is the regulator's concern, not the operators' daily concern" choice overlooks that operators carry the daily work that protects the community.

finalAssessment.prompt: Which pair best describes the bureaucratic style?
choices: Fast decisions and clear direction, but little input from the crew
High ownership and shared decisions, but slow to reach agreement
Consistent and auditable, but slow to adapt to unlisted cases
Great freedom for staff, but weak follow-up on their results
finalAssessment.explanation: Procedures and forms give consistency and an audit trail, and the weakness is rigidity and ticking boxes. The "Fast decisions and clear direction, but little input from the crew" choice describes the autocratic style. The "High ownership and shared decisions, but slow to reach agreement" choice describes the democratic style. The "Great freedom for staff, but weak follow-up on their results" choice describes the laissez-faire style.

finalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor holds a 25-minute one-on-one with each of 9 operators every two weeks. How many hours of one-on-ones is that in a 4-week month?
choices: 225 hours
15.0 hours
3.75 hours
7.5 hours
finalAssessment.explanation: One round = 9 x 25 = 225 minutes. Two rounds in 4 weeks = 450 minutes, and 450 / 60 = 7.5 hours. The "225 hours" choice counted one round only and labelled its 225 minutes as hours. The "15.0 hours" choice assumed weekly meetings, four rounds instead of two. The "3.75 hours" choice counted only one round of meetings in the month.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: At fictional Ridgeway Water, Pat is called crew chief. Pat assigns daily work, approves shift swaps and recommends discipline to the manager. Is Pat likely to be a supervisor in the legal sense?
choices: Yes, and the same test applies across jurisdictions without further checking
No, because the title is not supervisor and the title defines the role in law
No, because the manager takes the final disciplinary step, so Pat lacks authority
Likely yes, since real authority usually matters more than the title
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Legal tests generally look at what a person actually does, so Pat's duties point toward supervisor status. Employment law differs by jurisdiction. The "Yes, and the same test applies across jurisdictions without further checking" choice assumes the legal meaning is the same everywhere, which it is not. The "No, because the title is not supervisor and the title defines the role in law" choice puts the label ahead of the actual authority exercised. The "No, because the manager takes the final disciplinary step, so Pat lacks authority" choice overlooks that a recommendation the manager usually acts on can count as real authority even when approval sits higher.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional plant must have one operator on site 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Each operator is paid for a 36-hour week, and planning assumes 10 percent of paid hours go to leave and training. How many operators are needed, rounded up to a whole person?
choices: 7 operators
6 operators
4 operators
5 operators
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Hours = 24 x 7 = 168. Productive hours each = 36 x 0.90 = 32.4. Operators = 168 / 32.4 = 5.19, rounded up to 6. The "7 operators" choice divided the 168 weekly hours by the 24 hours in a day. The "4 operators" choice used 40-hour weeks and no allowance, then rounded down. The "5 operators" choice rounded 5.19 down, leaving a few hours uncovered each week.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A bureaucratic supervisor meets a problem the written procedure does not cover and says, "If it is not in the manual, we do not do it." The best response is to:
choices: Ignore the problem because the manual is the final word on what the crew does
Improvise a fix on the spot without telling anyone or recording it
Escalate the gap with the facts and ask for an update to the procedure
Blame the crew for finding a gap that the manual does not cover
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Rules give consistency, but a good supervisor notices their limits and feeds that back. The "Ignore the problem because the manual is the final word on what the crew does" choice lets a real problem stand because of a rigid reading of the rules. The "Improvise a fix on the spot without telling anyone or recording it" choice bypasses the process and leaves no record. The "Blame the crew for finding a gap that the manual does not cover" choice treats the finding as a fault rather than useful information.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A pump keeps tripping at a fictional station. What is the best way to start team troubleshooting?
choices: Ask each operator to work alone and report back with a view next week
Replace the pump at once, because it is the part everyone can see tripping
State the problem, gather facts on what changed and when, list causes
Wait a few days to see whether the pump stops tripping on its own
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: State, collect facts, list causes, test the likeliest in the safest way, agree roles and record what was tried. The "Ask each operator to work alone and report back with a view next week" choice loses the speed and shared knowledge of a team. The "Replace the pump at once, because it is the part everyone can see tripping" choice jumps to a fix without evidence of the cause. The "Wait a few days to see whether the pump stops tripping on its own" choice delays action and loses the chance to find a cause.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional operator, Kofi, spent 36 of his 40 paid hours hands-on. As supervisor he now spends 14 hours hands-on. How many hours per week moved away from hands-on work?
choices: 50 hours
22 hours
14 hours
2.6 hours
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Change = 36 - 14 = 22 fewer hands-on hours per week, which, with his paid week unchanged, go to assigning, coaching, scheduling and records. The "50 hours" choice added the two figures instead of finding the difference. The "14 hours" choice is the new hands-on time, not the change. The "2.6 hours" choice divided the old hours by the new hours, which gives a ratio, not a number of hours.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor finds that a 30-line checklist is ticked in bulk at the end of every shift. The best response is to:
choices: Sign lines as done, drop redundant ones, spot-check results
Add ten more lines to the list so that no step is ever missed
Accept the bulk ticking because the work usually gets done anyway
Stop using checklists and let operators rely on their memory instead
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Checklists signed as the work is done, cleared of redundant lines through the approved process (keeping required checks) and spot-checked get honest answers. A record nobody checks becomes a ritual. The "Add ten more lines to the list so that no step is ever missed" choice makes the list even harder to complete honestly. The "Accept the bulk ticking because the work usually gets done anyway" choice accepts a ritual that is easy to fake. The "Stop using checklists and let operators rely on their memory instead" choice removes the tool that shows what was done and when.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional utility has 63 operators. The manager wants a span of control of 7 per supervisor. How many supervisors are needed?
choices: 7 supervisors
56 supervisors
441 supervisors
9 supervisors
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Supervisors = 63 / 7 = 9. The "7 supervisors" choice confused the span with the number of supervisors. The "56 supervisors" choice subtracted 7 from 63 instead of dividing. The "441 supervisors" choice multiplied the two numbers instead of dividing.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Ten fictional operators each need 3 hours of training. The supervisor can release 2 operators per shift, and each released operator can attend the full 3-hour session in that shift. How many shifts are needed?
choices: 3 shifts
20 shifts
5 shifts
15 shifts
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Shifts = operators / released per shift = 10 / 2 = 5. The hours of training per person do not change the count of shifts. The "3 shifts" choice used the number of training hours as the number of shifts. The "20 shifts" choice multiplied 10 by 2 instead of dividing. The "15 shifts" choice multiplied the operators by the hours before dividing by the release rate.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor's close friend asks for the best shifts every month. Which response best fits the role?
choices: Refuse to discuss shifts with the friend to avoid any appearance of bias
Give the friend the best shifts, since it is a small favour
Set a written, fair method for assigning shifts, apply it to everyone and explain it
Let the crew fight it out among themselves each month
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A visible, consistent method answers the friend and the crew at once. The "Refuse to discuss shifts with the friend to avoid any appearance of bias" choice avoids the conversation instead of providing a clear, fair method. The "Give the friend the best shifts, since it is a small favour" choice creates favouritism that damages trust in the whole crew. The "Let the crew fight it out among themselves each month" choice leaves a supervisor's scheduling duty to chance and invites conflict.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: An operator wrote a wrong reading in the log and asks to erase it and write the correct one. The best supervisory response is to:
choices: Tear out the page and start a fresh one so the log looks neat
Correct it by the approved method: original readable, reason, date and initials
Allow the erasure because the correct number will be in the log, which is what matters
Leave the wrong reading uncorrected so that nobody is blamed for it
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A record is trusted when corrections are visible and explained rather than hidden. The "Tear out the page and start a fresh one so the log looks neat" choice destroys the record. The "Allow the erasure because the correct number will be in the log, which is what matters" choice hides the history of the record and weakens trust in it. The "Leave the wrong reading uncorrected so that nobody is blamed for it" choice keeps wrong data in the record and discourages honesty.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional crew has an annual budget of $320,000, and the plan assigns 15 percent of it to training and travel. How many dollars is that allocation?
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Share = 320,000 x 0.15 = 48,000 dollars. The percent is an assumption in this question, not a standard. The "$4,800" choice moved the decimal point one place too far. The "$305,000" choice treated 15 percent as a flat $15,000 and subtracted it instead of taking a percentage. The "$21,333" choice divided the budget by 15 instead of multiplying by 15 percent.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A supervisor announces a new log format in a quick meeting. Two weeks later half the crew still uses the old format. What is the best next step?
choices: Announce it again in the same quick way at the next shift meeting
Restate it in writing, ask for a say-back and check the next day's logs
Discipline everyone who kept using the old format, since they were told once
Accept both formats for now so that the crew is not upset by the change
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: A clear written expectation, a say-back check and a follow-up make a change stick. The "Announce it again in the same quick way at the next shift meeting" choice repeats the approach that failed. The "Discipline everyone who kept using the old format, since they were told once" choice punishes people before checking whether they understood the change and had the new format. The "Accept both formats for now so that the crew is not upset by the change" choice leaves the records inconsistent and hard to review.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which statement best describes the two directions of a supervisor's accountability?
choices: To the crew alone, because the crew is the group that does the actual work
To neither, because authority comes with the title and the pay grade
Up to the manager for results and down to the crew for fair direction
To the manager alone, because the crew has no claim on how the role is done
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: The middle position means looking both ways: a supervisor who looks only up becomes a messenger. The "To the crew alone, because the crew is the group that does the actual work" choice ignores accountability for results and records to the manager. The "To neither, because authority comes with the title and the pay grade" choice confuses authority with freedom from accountability. The "To the manager alone, because the crew has no claim on how the role is done" choice ignores the supervisor's duties of direction, training and fairness to the crew.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: The designated certified operator at a fictional facility will be on leave next week. The best supervisory step is to:
choices: Cancel the leave without discussing it with the person or the manager
Assume that any experienced operator can cover without checking the class needed
Wait until the person has left and then decide who should cover the shift
Check the rules on cover, tell the manager and arrange it before the leave
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Plan coverage ahead and confirm what the rules require; classes and substitution rules differ by jurisdiction. The "Cancel the leave without discussing it with the person or the manager" choice ignores the rules on cover and treats the person unfairly. The "Assume that any experienced operator can cover without checking the class needed" choice skips the question of whether the rule requires a particular certificate class. The "Wait until the person has left and then decide who should cover the shift" choice leaves the shift exposed to a coverage gap.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Two highly skilled specialists are upgrading a monitoring system and have a clear goal. Which approach best fits?
choices: Give them freedom to choose methods, set check-in points and keep the goal clear
Stay out of it and ask for nothing until the end
Make them follow the same checklist as a trainee
Direct each step and require approval before moving on
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Laissez-faire freedom works for experts with clear goals, as long as check-in points keep accountability. The "Stay out of it and ask for nothing until the end" choice leaves the supervisor without a way to see drift or problems. The "Make them follow the same checklist as a trainee" choice applies a rule meant for a different situation. The "Direct each step and require approval before moving on" choice wastes the experts' judgement and slows the project.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which note best documents an event involving a damaged hose?
choices: 14:10 hose cracked at fitting; operator said dropped; tagged out, manager told
Operator was careless with the hose and should really have known better by now
Hose was found to be broken again this week on the late shift
The crew keeps damaging equipment and nobody on the shift seems to care about it
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Facts, times, quotes and actions make a record useful and fair. The "Operator was careless with the hose and should really have known better by now" choice states an opinion and a conclusion without facts. The "Hose was found to be broken again this week on the late shift" choice gives only a rough time, does not describe the damage and records no action. The "The crew keeps damaging equipment and nobody on the shift seems to care about it" choice makes a sweeping claim with nothing to back it.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A newly promoted supervisor is unsure whether she can approve overtime. The best action is to:
choices: Let the crew vote on who works the overtime hours this month
Approve it, since supervisors normally control the crew's hours
Refuse any overtime request until the manager returns from leave
Ask the manager for written limits of her authority first
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Limits of authority differ by utility, so get them in writing and then use the authority you have. The "Let the crew vote on who works the overtime hours this month" choice passes a supervisor's decision to the group without checking the policy. The "Approve it, since supervisors normally control the crew's hours" choice assumes authority that the utility may reserve for a manager. The "Refuse any overtime request until the manager returns from leave" choice may leave the crew short; she should get the limits or reach the acting approver rather than refuse by default.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: Which example is usually called a water-associated pathogen concern, because exposure comes by a route other than drinking the water?
choices: Fluoride added at the plant at the wrong dose for the system's water
Dust and debris settling on the closed lid of a clean water storage tank
Bacteria from a sewage leak mixing with drinking water in a main
Legionella growing in warm building plumbing, inhaled in fine mist
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Some organisms grow in warm water systems and spread by inhalation of mist, so awareness reaches beyond drinking-water supply. The "Fluoride added at the plant at the wrong dose for the system's water" choice is a chemical dosing error, not a pathogen. The "Dust and debris settling on the closed lid of a clean water storage tank" choice is a surface cleanliness issue and not a described water-associated pathogen route. The "Bacteria from a sewage leak mixing with drinking water in a main" choice is a classic waterborne route through the drinking supply itself.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: What is the main risk of the paternalistic style?
choices: Staff may feel that nobody in charge really cares about them
Staff may become dependent and take criticism as a betrayal
The leader may follow the rulebook too strictly for new cases
Decisions may be left to the group and then not made in time
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Protection builds loyalty, but it can reduce independence and make honest feedback harder. The "Staff may feel that nobody in charge really cares about them" choice describes a cold style, not a protective one. The "The leader may follow the rulebook too strictly for new cases" choice describes the bureaucratic style. The "Decisions may be left to the group and then not made in time" choice describes the laissez-faire style, or a democratic process where nobody is assigned to decide.

alternateFinalAssessment.prompt: A fictional supervisor delegates 3 of 7 weekly tasks of 40 minutes each. Assuming 52 weeks in a year, how many hours per year does this free?
choices: 104 hours
6,240 hours
242.7 hours
2 hours
alternateFinalAssessment.explanation: Weekly saving = 3 x 40 = 120 minutes = 2 hours. Yearly = 2 x 52 = 104 hours. The "6,240 hours" choice left the number in minutes instead of converting to hours. The "242.7 hours" choice used all 7 tasks instead of the 3 that were delegated. The "2 hours" choice is the weekly saving and was not multiplied by 52 weeks.
